whyItExists.problem: Normal document flow stacks elements sequentially. Some UI elements need to escape flow — tooltips, modals, sticky headers, floating buttons — and sit relative to another element or the viewport.
whyItExists.solution: The position property lets elements break out of normal flow and be placed precisely using top, right, bottom, left coordinates relative to a chosen reference point.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Tooltips, modals, dropdown menus, sticky navigation, floating action buttons, overlapping UI effects.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't use positioning for standard page layouts — flexbox and grid are purpose-built for that and easier to maintain.

explainModes.beginner: Normally, elements sit where the browser puts them. Positioning lets you move elements somewhere specific — 'always stay at the top of the screen' (fixed) or 'sit 10px from the top of my parent' (absolute).
explainModes.simple: position: static (default, normal flow). relative (offset from its natural position). absolute (placed relative to its nearest positioned ancestor). fixed (placed relative to the viewport — stays while you scroll). sticky (stays in flow until it hits the scroll boundary, then sticks).
explainModes.standard: A positioned element (anything except static) creates a new stacking context for z-index. Absolute and fixed elements are removed from normal flow — other elements don't see them. Sticky is a hybrid: it behaves like relative until a scroll threshold, then fixed. z-index only works on positioned elements.
explainModes.technical: The stacking context determines z-index layering. A new stacking context is created by position != static with z-index != auto, transform, opacity < 1, filter, will-change, and others. Children cannot escape a stacking context's z-index layer — a child with z-index: 9999 cannot appear above a sibling whose parent has a lower stacking context.
explainModes.deepDive: The containing block for an absolutely positioned element is its nearest ancestor with position: relative, absolute, fixed, or sticky. If none exists, it's the initial containing block (the viewport). For fixed elements, a transformed ancestor creates a new containing block instead of the viewport — a common source of bugs when trying to position relative to the screen. CSS logical properties (inset-inline-start, inset-block-end) replace top/right/bottom/left for RTL-aware layouts.

content.text: Containing block — the anchor for absolute
A common z-index mistake: setting z-index on a non-positioned element (position: static) has no effect. The element must have position set to anything other than static.

questions.question: Which position value removes an element from normal flow and places it relative to the viewport?
questions.explanation: position: fixed removes the element from flow and places it relative to the viewport. It stays in position even when the page scrolls.

questions.question: For position: absolute to be positioned relative to a parent element, the parent must have position set to something other than static.
questions.explanation: Absolutely positioned elements are placed relative to their nearest ancestor that has position: relative, absolute, fixed, or sticky. Without this, they fall back to the initial containing block (the viewport).

faq.q: What is the difference between fixed and sticky?
faq.a: fixed is always relative to the viewport — it never moves. sticky starts in normal flow (like relative) and only sticks when scrolled to the specified threshold (top: 0). A sticky element is constrained to its scroll container; fixed is not.

Two common reasons: (1) the element has position: static — z-index only works on positioned elements. (2) A parent creates a stacking context with a lower z-index — children cannot escape their parent's stacking layer.

examples: GitHub's sticky file header in code review uses position: sticky
Every modal dialog uses position: fixed with a z-index overlay
Notification toasts (top-right corner) use position: fixed to stay on screen while content scrolls
